title: Evolution & Genetics · Episode 3
chapters: Evolution's leftovers: goosebumps, tailbones and the appendix

units.t: Evolution & Genetics. Episode three.
In this episode: Evolution's leftovers: goosebumps, tailbones and the appendix, Extinction and Gene editing and CRISPR.
Part one. Evolution's leftovers: goosebumps, tailbones and the appendix.
Your body carries traces of ancestors who had fur, tails and much bigger jaws.
Some leftovers have found new jobs; others are just along for the ride.
What vestigial means.
In The Descent of Man, published in 1871, Charles Darwin pointed to what he called rudimentary organs as evidence that humans share ancestry with other animals.
These were parts that seemed shrunken or purposeless in us but were fully functional in other species.
The modern term is vestigial.
It is often misunderstood as meaning completely useless.
Biologists use it more carefully: a vestigial structure has lost its original function, or much of it, though it may have gained a new one.
In the late 1800s some anatomists drew up long lists of supposedly useless organs.
Some items on those lists, such as the thymus, later proved essential.
Why we get goosebumps.
When you are cold or deeply moved by music, tiny muscles at the base of your hair follicles contract, pulling hairs upright and raising little bumps.
Each of these arrector pili muscles attaches to a single hair.
In heavily furred mammals the same reflex fluffs up the coat, trapping a thicker layer of insulating air.
It also makes an animal look bigger, which is why a frightened or angry cat puffs up.
Humans have lost most of our body fur, so the reflex achieves very little warmth or intimidation.
These muscles may still play a supporting role in hair growth, but the visible goosebump is largely a leftover.
The tail you once had.
At the base of your spine sits the coccyx, or tailbone, made of several small fused vertebrae.
It is what remains of the tail carried by our primate ancestors, and apes such as chimpanzees and gorillas lack an external tail too.
Human embryos make the connection vivid.
Around the fourth to sixth week of development an embryo has a distinct tail with more vertebrae than an adult keeps.
Later the tail stops growing and its extra cells are removed.
Yet the coccyx is not useless.
It anchors muscles, tendons and ligaments of the pelvic floor, and bears some of your weight when you lean back to sit.
The appendix rethought.
Darwin suggested the appendix was a shrunken remnant of a larger organ that helped ancestral primates digest leaves.
For over a century it was treated as a useless troublemaker, famous mainly for appendicitis, which can be life-threatening if the organ bursts.
The picture has changed.
The appendix is rich in lymphoid tissue, involved in immune defence.
Researchers have also proposed that it acts as a safe house for beneficial gut bacteria, helping repopulate the intestine after an illness such as severe diarrhoea.
Comparative studies suggest an appendix has evolved independently many times in different mammals, which hints at some advantage.
Even so, people who have it removed live normal, healthy lives.
Teeth, muscles and ears.
Our ancestors had larger jaws and chewed tougher food.
Human jaws became smaller over hundreds of thousands of years, a change many researchers link to cooking and softer diets.
Teeth shrank less, so wisdom teeth often find no room and can stay trapped, impaction, causing pain or infection.
A significant minority of people never develop one or more at all.
Touch your thumb to your little finger and flex your wrist: many people see a thin cord rise at the inner wrist.
That is the palmaris longus tendon.
Roughly one in seven people, varying between populations, lack it in one or both arms, with no noticeable loss of grip strength.
Small ear muscles, used by some animals to swivel their ears, survive too, and a few humans can still wiggle theirs.
The key idea: A vestigial structure has lost its original function, or much of it, but it is not necessarily useless.
Part two. Extinction.
Over 99% of all species that have ever lived are gone.
What wiped them out, and are we living through the next great loss?
Extinction is normal.
Extinction is the permanent loss of a species, and it is a normal part of life's history.
More than 99% of all species that have ever existed are now extinct.
A typical species lasts around one to ten million years in the fossil record, though some survive far longer.
What matters is the rate.
Most of the time, species vanish slowly, called background extinction.
One widely used estimate is roughly one extinction per million species per year.

Occasionally something far more dramatic happens: a mass extinction, often defined as the loss of at least three-quarters of Earth's species in a geologically short time, perhaps thousands to a few million years.
These events reshape life, clearing space for new groups.
The big five.
Scientists recognise five mass extinctions.
The end-Ordovician, about 445 million years ago, struck as ice ages dropped sea levels.
The Late Devonian, around 372 million, hit reefs and marine life.
The end-Permian, about 252 million, was the worst, wiping out roughly 90% of marine species.
The end-Triassic, 201 million, cleared the way for dinosaurs.
The end-Cretaceous, 66 million years ago, killed the non-bird dinosaurs and around three-quarters of all species.
The Permian and Triassic events coincide with enormous volcanic eruptions that released carbon dioxide, causing warming, ocean acidification and oxygen-starved seas.
The Cretaceous is linked to an asteroid about 10 kilometres wide striking near Chicxulub in Mexico, as huge Indian eruptions also ran.
Change faster than species can adapt or move is what kills.
Today's losses.
Today, extinctions are running far above the background rate.
A major 2019 global assessment by the scientific body IPBES estimated that around one million animal and plant species are threatened with extinction, many within decades.
The main drivers are habitat destruction, especially clearing land for farming, overhunting and overfishing, invasive species, pollution and climate change.
Whether this already counts as a 'sixth mass extinction' is debated: the losses so far are well short of three-quarters of species.
But many scientists warn that, at current rates, we could be heading that way.
Australia's losses.
Australia has one of the world's worst records for mammal extinctions.
Since 1788, more than 30 native mammals have been lost, including the lesser bilby and the pig-footed bandicoot.
The main culprits are feral cats and foxes, along with land clearing and changed fire patterns.
Small ground-dwelling mammals fared worst, and many survivors cling on in small pockets or on islands.
Some losses unfolded in plain sight.
The Christmas Island pipistrelle, a bat weighing a few grams, declined steeply through the 2000s.
A rescue was approved in July 2009, but searchers found only one bat.
Its last call was recorded on 26 August 2009.

The Bramble Cay melomys, a rodent on a tiny Torres Strait cay, was flooded repeatedly by rising seas and declared extinct in 2019, widely described as the first mammal lost to human-driven climate change.
What helps.
The news isn't all bad.
Conservation works when it tackles the real causes.
In Australia, fenced predator-free sanctuaries and islands cleared of cats, foxes and rats have allowed species like bilbies, bettongs and numbats to recover in places.
Lord Howe Island's rodent eradication, carried out in 2019, has helped native birds and insects rebound.
Individuals can help too: keep cats indoors or contained, choose native plants, support habitat protection, and report sightings of threatened species to citizen science programs.
Every species kept alive keeps options open for the future.
The key idea: More than 99% of all species that ever lived are extinct, so what matters is how fast species are being lost.
Part three. Gene editing and CRISPR.
A tool borrowed from bacteria now lets scientists rewrite DNA letter by letter.
It has already cured patients, and caused a scandal.
From bacteria to tool.
CRISPR began in bacteria.
Many store short snippets of viral DNA in a region of their genome called CRISPR.
If the virus returns, the bacterium makes RNA copies that guide cutting proteins, such as Cas9, to the matching viral DNA.
In the 2000s scientists realised this was an immune defence, and that reprogramming the guide could in principle direct the cut to almost any sequence.

In 2012 Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier showed CRISPR-Cas9 could be programmed to cut chosen DNA in a test tube, and within months teams including Feng Zhang's showed it worked in human cells.
Earlier tools, such as zinc finger nucleases and TALENs, were slow and costly to redesign for each target.
CRISPR was cheap, fast and flexible.
Doudna and Charpentier won the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
How the edit works.
The system has two main parts.
A short guide RNA, designed to match about 20 letters of target DNA, leads the Cas9 protein to the right spot in the genome.
Cas9 then cuts both strands of the DNA.
The cell rushes to repair the break.
Often the repair is sloppy, adding or deleting a few letters, which usually disables the gene.
If scientists also supply a template, the cell can sometimes copy it in, inserting a corrected sequence.
Newer versions, called base editing and prime editing, can change individual letters without fully cutting the DNA, making edits more precise.
Curing sickle cell.
The first approved CRISPR medicine, Casgevy, was approved in the United Kingdom in November 2023 and in the United States soon after.
It treats sickle cell disease and beta thalassaemia, inherited blood disorders caused by faulty haemoglobin.
Doctors collect a patient's blood stem cells and edit them to switch back on a form of haemoglobin normally made only before birth.
After chemotherapy clears the old bone marrow, the edited cells are returned.
Many trial patients became free of severe pain crises or regular transfusions.
The treatment is gruelling and extremely expensive, costing millions of dollars per patient.
Somatic versus germline.
Where the change is made matters.
Somatic editing changes cells in one patient, such as blood or liver cells, and isn't passed to children, like any other medical treatment.
Germline editing changes embryos, eggs or sperm, so every cell of the resulting person, and all their descendants, would carry the edit.
That raises deep questions of safety and consent, and Australia, like many countries, prohibits heritable changes to the human genome.
In November 2018, Chinese scientist He Jiankui announced the birth of twin girls from embryos edited to disable the CCR5 gene, aiming at HIV resistance.
A third edited child followed.
The edits were medically unnecessary and imprecise, and consent was a serious concern.
He was sentenced to three years in prison in 2019, and the case prompted calls for stronger oversight.
Crops, promise and questions.
Genetic modification of crops long predates CRISPR; the first GM food, a slow-softening tomato, went on sale in the US in 1994.
In Australia nearly all cotton is GM, and GM canola has been grown in several states since 2008, though Tasmania keeps a moratorium.
Since 2019, simple CRISPR edits that add no new DNA are not treated as GMOs.
Trials are testing treatments for inherited blindness, high cholesterol and rare liver diseases, and gene drives could spread edits through pests like malaria-carrying mosquitoes.
Questions remain: unintended edits, who can afford treatment, and where treating disease ends and enhancement begins.
When you read about a 'breakthrough', check whether it was in cells, animals or human trials, and whether it was peer reviewed.
The key idea: CRISPR is a bacterial immune system that scientists reprogrammed in 2012 to cut chosen DNA, winning the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What do biologists mean by a vestigial structure?
Answer. One that has lost much of its original function.
Question two. Since extinction is normal, what matters when judging today's losses?
Answer. How quickly species vanish compared with normal.
Question three. Where did the CRISPR system originally come from?
Answer. A bacterial defence against viruses.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
